title: Referrals and repeat work from existing clients
audience: Solo operators and team owners in a service business who want repeat bookings and referrals from clients they have already served.
learningOutcomes: Plan a review or referral request that is made after the client confirms the result and that the client can decline easily.
Write a next-service offer with a date, a scope and a price approach, and schedule the check-in that follows it.
Write referral reward terms, including the condition for payment, before any referral is made.

instruction.heading: Ask at the moment the client is most satisfied
instruction.body: The best time to ask for a review or referral is after the client has confirmed that the result is right, usually at sign-off or when the invoice is paid. Ask in one sentence, name the next step you would like, such as a review or the name of one person who might need the service, and make it easy to decline. Record what you asked and what the client said. Timing matters: in one Baylor Keller Center experiment, a late reminder brought in more reviews than an immediate one. Sending a review link or QR code is allowed, and Google provides one for this purpose. Do not write reviews for clients or invent them. Do not screen out unhappy clients in a way that hides complaints. Asking only happy clients is called review gating, and Podium, a review software vendor, says Google treats it as a violation. The ACCC's guidance on online reviews says incentives must be disclosed and must not depend on what the review says. Google also bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews, including for changing or removing negative reviews, so check each platform's terms before offering any incentive.

instruction.heading: Offer the next service before the client leaves
instruction.body: Repeat work is one of the most dependable sources of growth for a small service business. At the end of each job, propose the next step with a date: a fortnightly pool service, a quarterly carpet clean, an annual gutter and roof check, a spring garden plan, or a handyman visit to finish a list of items. Put the proposed scope, the interval and the price approach in writing, and confirm that the client agrees before you change their schedule. A written next step turns a passing comment into a booked job. If the written offer goes by email or text, check the electronic message rules first: ACMA's guidance indicates that inferred consent is narrow and does not cover a message sent just after a purchase.

instruction.heading: Check in at the interval that suits the service
instruction.body: Schedule a check-in after a period that suits the work. For a clean or a repair, a suggested starting point is about ninety days, which is a choice to test, not a benchmark. For a pool or a garden it may be after the next seasonal visit. The check asks whether the result still holds, whether anything has changed and whether there is other work to quote. Keep it short and useful, record what the client said, and close the loop with a reply. If the check is sent by email or text, check it against the electronic message rules in “Online presence: community groups, profiles and consent-based content”. A check-in that only asks about the result may not be commercial, but a message that promotes any service can be, even when it is framed as a reminder. ACMA's summary (read 2026-11-04) does not say whether one-to-one messages are covered, so check that point before you send.

instruction.heading: Re-contact previous clients before their busy periods
instruction.body: Many home-service needs follow the calendar: spring clean-ups, pool opening before the warm months, gutter checks before the wet season, garden work before holidays, and carpet cleaning before a lease handover. Plan a short message to previous clients a few weeks before each period. Offer the slots you can actually deliver, on written terms, with a clear way to opt out. Do not use the message to pressure anyone, and do not contact a client who has asked not to hear from you. ACMA's guidance says an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days, so record each opt-out as soon as you receive it and stop sending to that client. At the end of the period, review the response and note which timing worked.

instruction.heading: Set referral rewards in writing before anyone refers
instruction.body: A referral reward works best when the client knows the terms before they refer someone. Decide what you will offer, such as a credit on the next service or a small thank-you, and write down the condition for payment, which is normally that the referred person has completed a paid job. Tell the referrer the terms, keep a record of each referral and whether the reward was paid, and never promise a reward you cannot deliver. Keep the arrangement simple and fair. Research on referral programmes found that stating the referrer's reward in the invitation increased referrals in a set of studies, so say what the reward is in the invitation. Get the referred person's consent before any referral message is sent, because the referrer's word alone may not be enough. Check any cash-based reward, and its tax or contract effect, with an adviser before you start. No business.gov.au or ACCC guidance on referral rewards was found, so those points remain unconfirmed.

procedure: After each job is signed off, make one review or referral request and record what was asked and the answer.
Write the next-service offer with a date, scope, interval and price approach, and confirm it with the client.
Schedule the check-in for the interval that suits the service, and send it using the electronic message rules.
Plan a re-contact message for each busy period in the calendar, and exclude anyone who has opted out.
Write the referral reward terms and the payment condition before the first referral is made.
When a referral books, confirm the referred job is paid before applying the reward, and record the outcome.
Review at the end of each season which requests, offers and timings produced repeat work.

workedExamples.situation: A handyman completes a repair to a bathroom door for a regular client. She says she will recommend him to her sister, who lives in the same street. He wants to offer her a credit on her next job if the sister books.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should he do before the sister books, and what should he avoid?
workedExamples.reasoning: He writes down the reward terms before any referral happens: the credit, the condition that the sister completes a paid job, and when the credit will be applied. He asks his client to pass on the sister's details, and he contacts the sister only if she agrees. He does not promise a reward he has not written down. If he is unsure of the tax or contract effect of the credit, he confirms it with an adviser. He does not book any work outside his licence or insurance.

equipmentAndPpe: Client record with the sign-off date and the review or referral request made
Next-service offer template with scope, interval and price approach
Calendar of seasonal re-contact dates for the service
No PPE is needed for client follow-up; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Asking for a review before the client has confirmed the result.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask after sign-off or payment, when the client has confirmed the result is right.

commonErrors.error: Offering a referral reward that was never written down, so the terms are disputed later.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the reward and its payment condition before any referral is made, and give the referrer a copy.

commonErrors.error: Publishing a client's name, photo or review without their consent for that use.
commonErrors.prevention: Get consent for each thing you plan to publish, and keep the record.

commonErrors.error: Contacting a client who asked not to hear from you, or using a re-contact message to pressure them.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep an opt-out list, honour it at once, and keep re-contact messages factual and optional.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Publishing a client's name, photo, review or property detail needs the client's consent for that use. Do not write reviews on a client's behalf or invent them. If the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business, client details are also personal information; check the OAIC's small business guidance (summary read 2026-11-03) to see whether it applies to you.

Review platforms and referral programmes can have their own rules on incentives. Google bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews. The ACCC's guidance on online reviews says incentives must be disclosed and must not depend on the review's content. Check each platform's rules before offering any reward.

Check-in and re-contact messages sent by email or text can be commercial electronic messages under the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). A message that promotes any service can be commercial even when it is framed as a service reminder, and ACMA has been enforcing this area, so check each message before sending.

A referral does not extend the licence or authority of the business that accepts the work. Accept only the work your licence and insurance cover, in the state or territory where the work is done. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check the rules for each one you work in. This lesson does not grant any licence.

qualityStandard: Every review or referral request is made after sign-off or payment, and it includes an easy way to decline.
Every next-service offer is written, has a date and is confirmed by the client before the schedule changes.
Every referral reward has written terms and a payment condition, and is paid only when that condition is met.
documentationEvidence: Review or referral request log with the date sent and the answer.
Next-service offers with the date, scope, interval and client confirmation.
Referral reward terms with the referral record and payment outcome.
summary: Ask for reviews and referrals after the client has confirmed the result, and make it easy to say no.
Offer the next service in writing, with a date, before the client leaves.
Set referral rewards and their payment conditions in writing before anyone refers.

knowledgeChecks.question: When is the best time to ask a client for a review or referral?
options: Before the job starts, so the client feels committed
After the client has confirmed the result is right
Only when the client has sent you a complaint

knowledgeChecks.question: A client wants to publish a review with their name and a photo of the finished work. What do you need?
options: Their consent for the name and photo you plan to publish
Nothing, because the review is positive
Your own judgement that the photo looks professional

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a referral reward look like?
options: Paid to anyone who mentions your name
Decided after the referred person books, based on how keen the referrer seems
Decided and written in advance, with the condition for payment stated

knowledgeChecks.question: When does the lesson say to propose the next step for the client?
options: At the end of each job, with a date

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam
officialReferences.covers: Says commercial messages cannot be sent without the recipient's permission or consent; messages must accurately identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must contain an unsubscribe option under the Spam Act 2003, which the page says sets out responsibilities under Australian law. Does not mention one-to-one messages. Publisher: ACMA.
